essays.stem: Describe the tools and equipment used to mark out geometric shapes and patterns on sheet metal, and say what each one is used for.
essays.modelAnswer: A steel rule is used to measure and mark straight lengths, and a straight edge for long lines. A try square or combination square marks and checks lines at 90° to an edge, and a protractor marks and checks other angles. A scriber scratches fine, lasting lines on metal; a pencil or fine marker is used on bend lines. Dividers step off equal distances and scribe small arcs and circles, and trammels do the same for large ones. Odd-leg calipers scribe lines parallel to an edge. A centre punch marks centres for dividers and drilling, and a dot punch marks lines lightly so they can still be seen after cutting. Marking-out fluid is painted on so that scribed lines show up. A flat bench or surface table supports the sheet. Paper or card is used for trial patterns, and a calculator for the sums.
markingPoints: Steel rule or straight edge, square and protractor for lengths, right angles and angles
Scriber for cut lines, pencil or marker for bend lines
Dividers for small arcs and equal spacing; trammels for large arcs
Odd-leg calipers for parallel lines; centre or dot punch for centres and lines
Marking-out fluid, flat bench, and card for trial patterns

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to bisect a straight line and how to bisect an angle, using a compass and a straight edge.
essays.modelAnswer: To bisect a line AB, I open the compass to a little more than half the length of AB. With the point on A, I draw an arc above and below the line. Without changing the compass, I put the point on B and draw two more arcs that cross the first ones. I join the two crossing points with a straight line. This line cuts AB exactly in half and is at 90° to it. To bisect an angle, I put the compass point on the corner of the angle and draw an arc that cuts both arms. From each of these two points, with the same radius, I draw an arc so that the two arcs cross inside the angle. I draw a line from the corner through the crossing point. This line divides the angle into two equal parts. I check with a rule or a protractor that the two halves are equal.
markingPoints: Line: compass opened to more than half the line
Arcs drawn from each end with the same radius, crossing above and below
Joining the crossing points gives the bisector, at 90° to the line
Angle: arc from the corner cuts both arms; equal arcs from those points cross
Line from the corner through the crossing point; halves checked

essays.stem: Describe how to construct a regular hexagon with sides of 60 mm using a compass, and how you would check it.
essays.modelAnswer: The side of a regular hexagon is equal to the radius of the circle drawn around it. So I first draw a circle of 60 mm radius with a compass. I draw a centre line through the circle to give a starting point on its edge. Keeping the compass at 60 mm, I put the point on the starting point and mark an arc on the circle. Then I move the point to the new mark and step round again. I do this until there are six marks, and the last step should bring me back exactly to the starting point. I join the six marks with straight lines to form the hexagon. To check it, I measure each side, which should be 60 mm, and the distance across opposite corners, which should be 120 mm. I can also check the inside angles with a protractor: each should be 120°. If the last step does not land on the start, the compass has slipped, so I start again.
markingPoints: Knows the side equals the radius of the circle around it
Draws a circle of 60 mm radius
Steps the 60 mm radius round the circle six times
Joins the six points with straight lines
Checks: sides 60 mm, 120 mm across corners, angles 120°; redraws if it does not close

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to develop the pattern for a pipe that is cut off at an angle at one end (a truncated cylinder).
essays.modelAnswer: First I draw the front view, or elevation, of the pipe with the sloping cut at the top, and below it the plan, which is a circle of the pipe's diameter. I divide the plan circle into 12 equal parts and number the points. I project each point up to the elevation to give 12 lines along the pipe, each ending at the sloping cut. Beside the elevation I draw a stretch-out line equal to the circumference (π × diameter) and divide it into the same 12 equal parts, numbering them in the same order, starting at the seam. I draw a line up from each division. From each point where a line meets the sloping cut in the elevation, I project across to the line with the same number on the pattern. I join these points with a smooth curve. Then I add the lap or seam allowance on one end. I check the pattern by cutting it out in card and rolling it.
markingPoints: Draws the elevation with the sloping cut, and the plan circle
Divides the plan into 12 equal parts and projects them to the elevation
Stretch-out line equal to the circumference, divided and numbered the same way
Projects the heights across and joins the points with a smooth curve
Adds the seam allowance and checks the pattern in card

essays.stem: Describe how to develop the pattern for a frustum of a right cone (a cone with its top cut off), such as a small hopper.
essays.modelAnswer: First I draw the elevation of the frustum full size, or to scale, showing the top and bottom diameters and the height. I extend the two sloping sides upwards until they meet at the point of the full cone, called the apex. With the compass point on the apex, I draw two arcs: one with a radius equal to the slant length from the apex to the bottom edge, and one with a radius to the top edge. The length of the outer arc must equal the circumference of the base, π × diameter. I can find it by dividing the base circle into 12 parts and stepping 12 of these lengths along the outer arc, or by working out the sector angle: base radius ÷ slant height of the full cone × 360°. I draw lines from the apex to each end of the outer arc. The shape between the two arcs and the two lines is the pattern. I add the allowance for the seam, then check it in card.
markingPoints: Draws the elevation and extends the sides to find the apex
Draws arcs from the apex using the slant lengths to the bottom and the top edges
Makes the outer arc equal to the base circumference (stepped divisions or sector angle)
Joins the ends of the arc to the apex to complete the shape
Adds the seam allowance and checks in card

essays.stem: Explain why allowances are added to sheet metal patterns, and describe three kinds of allowance.
essays.modelAnswer: Allowances are extra metal added to a pattern so that the edges can be joined, made stiffer or made safe. Without them the finished job would be too small or could not be joined. A lap allowance is added to one edge so that the two edges overlap, for example for riveting, spot welding or soldering a seam. A grooved or folded seam allowance is added to both edges so that they can be folded, hooked together and locked flat. A wired edge allowance is added to an open edge so it can be rolled around a wire, which makes the edge stiff and takes away the sharp edge. A safe edge, or hem, is folded over to make the edge stiff and safe to handle. A flange allowance lets the job be bolted or joined to another part. The size of each allowance depends on the joint and the sheet thickness, and is taken from the drawing or the Centre's tables.
markingPoints: Why: extra metal so edges can be joined, stiffened or made safe; job would otherwise be undersize
Lap allowance described
Grooved or folded seam allowance described
Wired edge, safe edge (hem) or flange allowance described
Size depends on the joint and sheet thickness, from the drawing or tables

essays.stem: A cylindrical tank body, 600 mm outside diameter and 800 mm high, is to be rolled from 3 mm steel plate. Explain how you would work out the size of plate needed, showing your working.
essays.modelAnswer: The tank body is a cylinder, so the flat plate is a rectangle. Its width is the height of the tank, 800 mm. Its length must equal the circumference measured at the middle of the plate thickness, because the outside of the plate stretches and the inside squeezes when it is rolled. The outside diameter is 600 mm and the plate is 3 mm thick, so the mean diameter is 600 − 3 = 597 mm. The length is π × mean diameter = 3.142 × 597, which is about 1876 mm. So the plate for the body is about 1876 mm × 800 mm. If the seam is to be lapped rather than butt welded, I add the lap allowance to the length. I would check my sums on a calculator and confirm with the drawing or the supervisor that 600 mm is the outside diameter, because an inside diameter would give a different mean diameter.
markingPoints: The plate is a rectangle with a width equal to the height (800 mm)
Uses the mean diameter, and says why (outside stretches, inside squeezes)
Mean diameter = 600 − 3 = 597 mm
Length = π × 597 ≈ 1876 mm
Adds any lap allowance and confirms whether the diameter is inside or outside

essays.stem: Describe how to construct angles of 90°, 45° and 30° using only a compass and a straight edge.
essays.modelAnswer: To make 90° at a point P on a line, I put the compass point on P and draw an arc cutting the line on both sides of P. From each of these two points, with the compass opened wider, I draw arcs above the line so that they cross. A line from P through the crossing point is at 90° to the first line. To make 45°, I bisect this 90° angle. With the point on P, I draw an arc cutting both arms, then from each of those points I draw arcs that cross, and join P to the crossing. To make 30°, I first make 60°. I draw an arc from P cutting the line, then with the same radius I put the point where the arc cuts the line and mark the arc again. A line from P through this mark is at 60°. Then I bisect the 60° angle to give 30°. I check each angle with a protractor.
markingPoints: 90°: arcs from P cut the line both sides; wider arcs cross; join to P
45°: bisect the 90° angle
60°: step the same radius once along the arc from the base line
30°: bisect the 60° angle
Checks each angle with a protractor

essays.stem: Explain how to transfer a paper pattern onto sheet steel, cut it out and roll it into a cylinder, including the safety points.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the paper or card pattern against the drawing and test it if I can. I lay the steel sheet on a flat bench and place the pattern close to an edge to save metal, then clamp or weight it so it cannot move. I scribe round it on the cut lines, use a pencil or marker on any bend lines, and centre punch any hole centres. I cut straight edges with straight snips or the guillotine and curves with curved-cut snips, cutting just outside the line and keeping my other hand clear of the blades. I file or deburr all the edges. To form the cylinder, I roll it slowly in the bending rolls, or round a pipe, a little at a time, checking the curve with a template until the edges meet. Then I join the seam as the drawing says. I wear gloves when handling and cutting sheet, but keep hands and gloves well clear of the rolls. I wear safety glasses when cutting and filing, and put offcuts in the scrap bin, as their edges are very sharp.
markingPoints: Checks the pattern; places it to save metal and clamps or weights it
Scribes cut lines, pencil on bend lines, punches centres
Cuts with the right snips just outside the line, and deburrs
Rolls a little at a time, checking with a template, then joins the seam
Safety: gloves for sheet but clear of the rolls, safety glasses, hands clear of blades, offcuts in scrap bin

essays.stem: Explain why accuracy matters when developing patterns, and describe the checks you would make before and after cutting.
essays.modelAnswer: Patterns must be accurate because any error is carried into the finished job. If a pattern is a few millimetres short, a cylinder will not close and the seam will gap. If it is too long, the edges overlap and the diameter is wrong. Parts that do not fit must be made again, which wastes steel, time and money. Before cutting, I check the drawing sizes and my calculations twice, check the construction lines and angles with a rule, square and protractor, and check that the right allowances are on the right edges. Where possible I make a trial pattern in card and fit it. I check the pattern marked on the sheet against the drawing before the first cut. After cutting and forming, I measure the main sizes, such as the diameter in several places, the height and the angle of any cut. I check that the seams meet evenly and compare the job with the drawing. Any error is reported and put right before the parts are joined or welded.
markingPoints: Why: errors carry into the job, causing poor fit and waste of material, time and money
Before cutting: check sizes and calculations twice
Check constructions, angles and allowances
Trial pattern in card; check the marked-out sheet against the drawing
After forming: measure main sizes, check seams, compare with the drawing, report errors

practical1.title: Construct and cut out geometric shapes in sheet steel
practical1.brief: Each member constructs and cuts out two shapes from 0.8 mm mild steel sheet, using a steel rule, square, dividers or compass and scriber, with a protractor for checking. The assessor shares out the shapes, for example: a regular hexagon with 50 mm sides; a regular octagon drawn in a 100 mm square; an equilateral triangle with 100 mm sides; a 100 mm diameter disc with its edge divided into 12 equal parts and centre punched; and a plate with a 90°, a 45° and a 30° angle constructed on it. First, as a group, read the shape cards and plan the layout on the sheet so that little metal is wasted. Then each member: (1) paints marking-out fluid on their area and uses a straight datum edge; (2) constructs their shapes with compass and rule, leaving the construction lines visible; (3) has another member check the sizes and angles; (4) cuts the shapes out with snips, just outside the line; (5) files and deburrs the edges; (6) checks the finished shapes against the card. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Mild steel sheet, 0.8 mm thick, about 600 mm × 300 mm for the group
Steel rule, try square, scriber, dividers or compass, centre punch and protractor
Shape cards from the assessor, and paper for practice
photos: The group's layout plan for the shapes on the sheet
A member's shapes constructed on the sheet, with the construction lines showing
Another member checking the sizes and angles with a rule and protractor
A shape being cut out with snips
All the finished shapes laid out with their shape cards
The work area cleaned, with offcuts in the scrap bin
checklist: Planned the layout with the group to save metal
Used marking-out fluid and a straight datum edge
Constructed the shapes correctly with compass and rule, leaving construction lines visible
Sizes within about ±1 mm and angles within about ±1° of the card
Checked another member's work fairly and accurately
Cut the shapes cleanly with the right snips, keeping hands clear of the blades
Handled the sheet safely and put offcuts in the scrap bin
safety: Wear gloves when handling and cutting sheet: the edges are very sharp
Wear safety glasses when cutting and filing
Keep the hand that holds the sheet away from the snip blades
Put sharp offcuts straight into the scrap bin; never leave them on the floor or bench
Keep scribers and dividers pointing down, or with a cover on the point, when not in use

practical2.title: Develop, make and check a truncated cylinder and a cone frustum
practical2.brief: As a group, develop the patterns for two items and make them in thin sheet metal: (A) a pipe of 100 mm diameter, 150 mm high on its long side, cut at 45° at the top (a truncated cylinder, by the parallel line method); and (B) a cone frustum with a 150 mm base diameter, a 75 mm top diameter and a 100 mm vertical height (by the radial line method). Share out the stages so that each member leads at least one and everyone takes part: (1) draw the elevation and plan of each item full size on paper; (2) divide the plans into 12 parts and work out the circumference and the stretch-out, or the sector, by calculation, with another member checking the sums; (3) project the points and draw each development, adding a 10 mm lap allowance on one edge; (4) cut the patterns in card, roll them and check that they match the drawing; (5) transfer the patterns to 0.6 mm sheet, cut them out and deburr them; (6) roll each item, join the lap with blind rivets (or as the assessor directs) and check the sizes. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Drawing paper, card, pencil, eraser, compass, rule, set squares, protractor and a calculator
Thin sheet metal, 0.6 mm (galvanised or mild steel), enough for both items
Scriber, dividers, steel rule and marking-out fluid
Straight-cut and curved-cut snips, and files
Bending rolls, or a length of pipe to form the sheet round
Blind rivet tool and blind rivets, and a drill with a suitable bit
The assessor's drawing of both items
photos: The elevations and plans drawn full size, with the plans divided into 12
The calculations for the circumference and the cone sector, checked
The finished paper developments, with the lap allowance shown
The card trial models rolled up next to the drawing
The patterns marked out on the sheet metal
The two finished items, joined, with a rule showing the main sizes
The work area cleaned, with offcuts in the scrap bin
checklist: Drew the elevation and plan accurately and full size
Divided the plan into 12 equal parts and projected the points correctly
Worked out the circumference or the sector angle correctly
Drew a smooth, accurate development with the lap allowance on the right edge
Tested the pattern in card and made any corrections
Transferred, cut and deburred the sheet pattern neatly
Formed and joined the item so the seam meets evenly and the sizes match the drawing (within about 2 mm)
Took a full part in the group and checked others' work
safety: Wear gloves when handling and cutting sheet: the edges are very sharp
Wear safety glasses when cutting, drilling and riveting
Keep fingers clear of the bending rolls and the snip blades, and keep loose gloves away from the rolls
Clamp the sheet when drilling rivet holes; never hold it by hand
Put offcuts in the scrap bin straight away
